principal_characters: the would-be Lord of Tartary; the Lady Caroline ('Lovelocks'); Marjorie May, Madeleine Rose, Humphrey John and Emmanuel ('O Dear Me!'); the sailorman and Jenny ('The Silver Penny'); the gnomies; the Ogre and the singing mother; Dame Hickory; Captain Lean; the child in the story
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the Georgian lyric manner: the rhymed stanza of four or eight lines, the plain monosyllabic diction, the observed countryside and the elegiac undertone, without the modernist break in syntax. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is the lyric of the half-heard and the unseen.
historical_context: The Edwardian nursery and the golden age of the illustrated children's book. The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1901 and first published in 1902 and the corpus places it within Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the golden-age tale; georgian anthology lyric.
literary_significance: Songs of Childhood is the first book of the greatest English writer of children's verse: published under the pseudonym Walter Ramal, it began the body of nursery poetry that Peacock Pie would perfect, and it is one of the permanent children's books in English.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Walter John de la Mare. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1902, as children's poetry collection (as walter ramal), by Walter de la Mare. Composed between 1899 and 1901. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Eminent Victorians
description: The book that invented modern biography: Manning, Florence Nightingale, Arnold and General Gordon, reduced to human size. It is a prose work of 1918 by Lytton Strachey; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under biography and the modern life; critical essay and the modern review and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Strachey's four short lives — Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Thomas Arnold of Rugby and General Gordon — use irony, psychology and the revealing scene to dismantle the Victorian ideal of the great man, and the book ends with Gordon's death at Khartoum.
narrative_structure: Four separate lives, each with a preface and a short bibliography. A documented life in chapters, told with the scene and dialogue of the novelist and the quotation from the papers. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
principal_characters: Cardinal Manning; Florence Nightingale; Thomas Arnold; General Gordon
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the new biography: the documented life told with the novelist's scene and dialogue, the quotation from letters and papers, and the psychological interpretation offered as inference rather than as assertion. The author's characteristic manner is the short, ironic, epigrammatic life.
historical_context: The First World War, which had destroyed the Victorian world the book dismantles, and the Bloomsbury reaction against Victorian earnestness. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1918 and first published in 1918 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under biography and the modern life; critical essay and the modern review.
literary_significance: Eminent Victorians invented modern biography: its irony, its psychological penetration and its use of the revealing detail changed how lives are written, and every twentieth-century biographer who debunks or humanises a subject works in its debt.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Giles Lytton Strachey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Chatto and Windus in London in May 1918 and by G. P. Putnam's Sons in New York the same year; the four lives had appeared in The Cornhill and The New Statesman between 1913 and 1917. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Queen Victoria
description: The finest short life in English: Victoria, Albert, Melbourne and Disraeli, and the private life behind the public monument. It is a prose work of 1921 by Lytton Strachey; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under biography and the modern life and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Strachey follows Victoria from a lonely childhood through the accession, the domination of Lord Melbourne, the marriage to Albert, the widowhood of forty years, the highland servant John Brown, the Indian secretary Disraeli and the Diamond Jubilee, ending with her death in 1901.
narrative_structure: Ten chapters from 1819 to 1901, with an epilogue. A documented life in chapters, told with the scene and dialogue of the novelist and the quotation from the papers.
principal_characters: Queen Victoria; Prince Albert; Lord Melbourne; Disraeli; John Brown; the Duchess of Kent
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the new biography: the documented life told with the novelist's scene and dialogue, the quotation from letters and papers, and the psychological interpretation offered as inference rather than as assertion. The author's characteristic manner is the short, ironic, epigrammatic life.
historical_context: The Victorian age and its aftermath, and the Bloomsbury reaction against the public pieties of the previous century. The record dates the work as composed in 1920 and first published in 1921 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under biography and the modern life.
literary_significance: Queen Victoria is the most admired short life in English and won the James Tait Black Prize: it made the Victorian age intelligible as a private life and established the modern literary biography as an art.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Giles Lytton Strachey. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Chatto and Windus in London in May 1921 and by Doubleday, Page in New York the same year; it received the James Tait Black Memorial Prize. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Vision and Design
description: The book that brought modern art into English criticism: the formalist essay and the case for Post-Impressionism. It is a prose work of 1920 by Roger Fry; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under critical essay and the modern review.
plot_or_argument: The essays — 'An Essay in Aesthetics', 'Art and Socialism', 'The Art of the Bushmen', 'Negro Sculpture', 'Giotto', 'The French Post-Impressionists' — argue for the primacy of form over subject and defend the art that Fry had exhibited in 1910 and 1912.
narrative_structure: Twenty-five essays written over twenty years, arranged thematically. An essay of criticism: the thesis, the quotation examined, the comparison and the judgement, with the personal voice admitted into the argument.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of criticism: the essay as an argument with a thesis, the quotation examined at length, the comparison and the judgement, and the personal voice admitted into the critical sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the formalist description of a picture — line, mass, colour and the organisation of the surface.
historical_context: The Post-Impressionist exhibitions of 1910 and 1912, the Bloomsbury art world, and the English resistance to modern art. The record dates the work as composed between 1909 and 1919 and first published in 1920 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under critical essay and the modern review.
literary_significance: Vision and Design made modern art intelligible to English readers: its formalism gave English criticism a method, its defence of Post-Impressionism changed the taste of a generation, and it is the founding book of modern English art criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Roger Eliot Fry. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1920, as art criticism (essays), by Roger Fry. Composed between 1909 and 1919. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Pointed Roofs
description: The first English stream-of-consciousness novel: a young woman goes to Germany to teach and the world is rendered from inside her mind. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by Dorothy Richardson; it belongs to The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness and it is catalogued here under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
plot_or_argument: Miriam Henderson, a shabby-genteel English girl of seventeen, goes to a German finishing school to teach English. The novel records her impressions — the school, the town, the other teachers, the music, the humiliation and the freedom — entirely through her consciousness, in the continuous present of perception.
narrative_structure: Continuous present-tense interior monologue in thirteen chapters. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
principal_characters: Miriam Henderson; the Fräulein; the school; the German town
literary_form: Novel (first of Pilgrimage); novel of consciousness
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the interior monologue uninterrupted by an explaining narrator.
historical_context: The English and German boarding schools of the 1890s, and the restricted life of the educated but poor woman of the period. The record dates the work as composed between 1913 and 1914 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
literary_significance: Pointed Roofs is the first English stream-of-consciousness novel, preceding Ulysses by seven years: it gave English fiction the sustained interior monologue, and it is the founding text of the novel of female consciousness that Woolf and Mansfield would develop.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Dorothy Miller Richardson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1915, as novel (first of pilgrimage), by Dorothy Richardson. Composed between 1913 and 1914. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Good Soldier: A Tale of Passion
description: The most perfect English novel of the period: a study of deception told by a narrator who is himself deceived. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by Ford Madox Ford; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: John Dowell, a wealthy American, recounts the nine years he and his wife Florence spent at Nauheim with their friends Edward and Leonora Ashburnham — the 'good soldier' of the title — and slowly reveals the adulteries, the lies and the cruelties beneath the surface, including his own blindness and Florence's suicide.
narrative_structure: Four parts in a broken chronology narrated by Dowell, with deliberate repetitions and withholdings.
principal_characters: John Dowell; Florence Dowell; Edward Ashburnham; Leonora Ashburnham; Nancy Rufford; Maisie Maidan
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the impressionist method: the scene rendered as it strikes a mind, in broken chronology, with the narrator's hesitations left in.
historical_context: The Edwardian upper class and its conventions, the European spa of the pre-war years, and the code of honour that conceals everything. The record dates the work as composed between 1913 and 1914 and first published in 1915 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England; The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness, it is catalogued under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; experimental novel and the modernist form.
literary_significance: The Good Soldier is the most perfect English novel of the period and the great novel of unreliable narration: its broken chronology, its narrator's self-deception and its famous opening — 'this is the saddest story I have ever heard' — made it the model for the modern novel of deception.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ford Hermann Hueffer. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by John Lane in London on 27 March 1915 under the title The Saddest Story; the title was altered at the publisher's insistence during the war. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Some Do Not…
description: The first volume of the great English war tetralogy: Christopher Tietjens, the last Tory, and the end of Edwardian England. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by Ford Madox Ford; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Christopher Tietjens, a brilliant statistician in the Imperial Department of Statistics, is married to the unfaithful Sylvia and in love with Valentine Wannop, a suffragette. The novel moves between the golf course at Rye, the London of the war office and the trenches of the Western Front in 1917, and ends with Christopher's return to England and the collapse of his marriage.
narrative_structure: Two parts: the pre-war England and the Western Front of 1917. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
principal_characters: Christopher Tietjens; Sylvia Tietjens; Valentine Wannop; Vincent Macmaster; General Campion; Mrs Duchemin
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the impressionist method: the scene rendered as it strikes a mind, in broken chronology, with the narrator's hesitations left in.
historical_context: Edwardian England before 1914 and the Western Front of 1917, the suffrage movement and the official class. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1924 and first published in 1924 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England; Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
literary_significance: Some Do Not… opens the greatest English war novel: its portrait of Christopher Tietjens as the last English gentleman, its technical brilliance and its picture of a society destroying itself made Parade's End the finest English novel of the war and the transition to modern England.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ford Hermann Hueffer. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by John Lane in London in April 1924. The record grades the work as major canon.
